READING

**The structural constraint both courses share**

In-river works take six weeks. The permitted window opens 1 July. Works begun in July complete around mid-August; the certificate follows within six weeks, arriving in late September at the earliest. The renewal must be lodged by 2027-05-31. Those two events cannot be brought into the right sequence without either a derogation or a substituted undertaking. Both courses accept that; the question is which substitution is safer.

**What PENNYQUAY actually delivers on the bank dimension**

PENNYQUAY files with a dated undertaking. The Board has accepted this mechanism before. But it has also been entirely consistent: Cadgarth (2024) and Nant Elwy (2025) both used that route and both received six-year renewals, not fifteen. No counter-example is offered. A six-year renewal from 2028 expires in 2034. The loan runs to 2039. That is a five-year gap, and it is precisely what the bank identified on 2026-06-22 as grounds for putting the facility under review. PENNYQUAY does not avoid the bank risk; it delivers it with near-certainty. The outage saving (£8,436 against £19,152) and the absence of a deposit are real advantages, but they are denominated in thousands. A facility review on a £480,000 loan is denominated in multiples of that, especially for a two-person operation with no margin to absorb a covenant breach, an accelerated repayment demand, or a punitive refinancing requirement.

**What LINTHAUGH actually risks**

If the derogation is refused on 2027-01-25, the £46,000 deposit is forfeit and the £9,000 application fee is spent. That is £55,000 lost, and the fallback is the undertaking route—the same outcome as PENNYQUAY but £55,000 worse. That is the genuine downside.

Three things limit that downside substantially.

First, the Rivers Board's own published refusal notices identify the decisive variable: every refused scheme had no dated regulatory driver. Blaenclydach has the most precisely dated regulatory driver possible—a statutory renewal deadline (2027-05-31), a legal requirement for a compliance certificate as a condition of that renewal, a legal requirement for works as a condition of the certificate, and a legal requirement for a derogation as a condition of the works. The chain is documented and the dates are fixed. This is structurally different from all seven refusals.

Second, the 4/11 base-rate applies to a pool that includes all seven schemes without a dated driver. Among schemes that do have one, the implied success rate is much higher—possibly all four grants. Blaenclydach sits squarely in that group.

Third, the timing arithmetic still works in the failure scenario. Eighteen weeks from 2027-01-25 lands on 2027-05-31, the renewal deadline. The fallback is tight but viable. A refusal does not close the undertaking route.

**The cost differential in context**

The extra outage from February versus July is £10,716. The £46,000 deposit, if the works proceed, is a payment on account of the contract; if they do not, it is forfeited. Both are real commitments. But the extra revenue impact of running on a six-year licence—and the financial consequence of a bank review during those years—is not bounded the way these figures are. A facility under review can escalate incrementally through tightened covenants and increased margin, or acutely through acceleration. Either trajectory is worse than £55,000.

**The fallback under LINTHAUGH**

An important structural point: PENNYQUAY's outcome (undertaking, probable six-year renewal, bank review) is also LINTHAUGH's worst-case outcome, reached only after paying £55,000 more. PENNYQUAY's best-case outcome is the same thing. LINTHAUGH's best-case outcome—a complete filing, a fifteen-year renewal expiring 2043, four years past the loan—is not available under PENNYQUAY at all, because the July slot cannot deliver a certificate before 31 May regardless of how the rest of the timetable is arranged.

**Summary of the bet**

PENNYQUAY is not a cautious choice; it is a certain walk into the outcome the bank has already flagged in writing. LINTHAUGH stakes a defined sum (£55,000 in the failure scenario) against a risk that is both near-certain and potentially existential under PENNYQUAY, at odds that are materially better than the raw 4/11 rate because Blaenclydach possesses the one factor the Board has consistently cited as the distinction between grants and refusals. The deposit commitment before the decision is the hardest part, but it is the price of access to the only route that produces a fifteen-year renewal. That bet should be taken.

---

READING
The structural logic is as above. PENNYQUAY near-certainly produces a six-year renewal; that near-certainly triggers the bank's stated concern about the facility. LINTHAUGH carries a bounded downside of £55,000 and a well-founded application—Blaenclydach has precisely the dated regulatory driver that the Board's own refusal notices identify as the dividing line—with a successful outcome being the only path to a fifteen-year renewal that outlasts the loan.

CALL
LINTHAUGH

GROUNDS
PENNYQUAY delivers a six-year renewal with near-certainty—exactly the outcome the bank has warned in writing will put the £480,000 facility under review—whereas LINTHAUGH's derogation application rests on the one factor the Board has consistently cited as distinguishing every grant from every refusal, and its success is the only route to a fifteen-year renewal that covers the loan term and removes the bank risk entirely, making the £55,000 downside of a refused derogation a proportionate stake against an existential lending exposure.
